Fusion is a build-time oriented, reflectionless Java framework. You declare models and beans with plain annotations, and an annotation processor generates the wiring, codecs and configuration binding at compile time - only bean resolution happens at runtime. This keeps applications light and GraalVM-native friendly.

Fusion HTTP Client is based on java.net.http.HttpClient. It is configured with ExtendedHttpClientConfiguration which enables to:
optionally provide a configured HttpClient instance - otherwise the default JVM one is used,
optionally provide a set of RequestListeners which listen for requests.
Request listener is a callback triggered before and after each request. It enables to store data before the requests in the caller context and execute some callback once the request is finished. To pass data between both steps (since the request can be asynchronous or not) it uses a State which can hold any data the listener needs.

The HTTP stack of Fusion is built on Apache Tomcat (server) and java.net.http (client), with a uniform request/response API and generated endpoint matchers.
JSON-RPC is a first-class, core feature: declare a @JsonRpc method on any bean and it is served over HTTP with full OpenRPC discovery - no routing or serialization plumbing to write. It is the recommended way to expose an API and shines for internal backends.
Besides RPC, the same server serves plain Endpoint/@HttpMatcher handlers and health/metrics, the client is an extended java.net.http with listeners, routing and replay, and tracing bridges both sides.
JSON-RPC - JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP with @JsonRpc methods, pre-request hooks and OpenRPC support.
HTTP server - Tomcat abstraction, health checks and metrics, high level Endpoint API

An operator is generally a process handling Custom Resource Definition (CRD). In other words, it is a process handling custom descriptor types.
A common example is to handle an API kind of descriptor instead of creating a ConfigMap plus a Deployment plus an Ingress plus a LoadBalancer:
as for Yupiik Bundlebee, we prefer to use descriptors in JSON since it is easier to work with and less error prone.
Once deployed, the operator will be responsible to convert the spec in Kubernetes default objects (Deployment, ...). On the user side you can manage your API with any Kubernetes API client, including kubectl: kubectl get -n my-apps my-apis.

A span is created by an evaluator (Supplier<Span>) which provides the parent span, optionally over the request. Traces are aggregated by an AccumulatingSpanCollector which you combine with a flusher (ZipkinFlusher or OpenTelemetryFlusher) to send spans to a collector. Identifiers are provided by an IdGenerator - use IdGenerator.Type.HEX for Zipkin. A Clock is used to timestamp spans and compute their duration.
the accumulator should generally be closed if you reuse AccumulatingSpanCollector.
TracingValve is added to the Tomcat pipeline to trace incoming requests:
if you reuse AccumulatingSpanCollector, it is automatically closed with the valve "stop" phase. You can combine the accumulator with ZipkinFlusher or OpenTelemetryFlusher onFlush implementation to flush to a zipkin collector v2.
